correctness.rationale: For every period dividing q, Proposition 4.6 of Huang–Jenkinson–Xu–Zhang bounds each invariant digit frequency by alpha, hence its integer q-block digit count by floor(q alpha). The rational upper mechanical q-block attains this count and all its rotations are lexicographically beta-admissible: every k-prefix has at most ceil(k p/q) <= ceil(k alpha) ones. For coprime p,q, Borel–Laubie extremality of lower Christoffel words implies every other q-word with p ones has a lexicographically larger maximal rotation. The q-1 prefix agreement under 0<alpha-p/q<q^-2 then excludes that rotation; integer composition forbids its sole difference at position q-1. This proves exact uniqueness up to shifts. Standard continued-fraction approximation gives infinitely many qualifying denominators. Reproducible exact-integer enumeration tests the finite comparisons but is not a substitute for these arguments.

originality.rationale: The October 2026 primary source establishes global alpha digit maximality and constructs some return-loop periodic approximants, but does not classify the exact constrained optimum at every q or unique maximizing q-periodic orbit near lower reduced rational approximations. The classical Borel–Laubie Christoffel extremal ordering is credited as a crucial input; its statement concerns cyclic words with fixed digit content, not admissibility in irrational Sturmian beta-shifts. Sidorov’s survey studies different balanced-word optimization problems. The examined published and historical claim summaries did not state a covering dynamical rigidity theorem. An equivalent undocumented reformulation in beta-shift combinatorics remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: The nearest input theorem (Borel–Laubie) is classical. An unindexed older beta-shift application of that extremality could contain the same finite-period implication.

value.rationale: The constrained extremal digit average at each finite period, its exact Diophantine deficit, and the rigidity of optimal periodic orbits on infinitely many lower-convergent periods are natural dynamical questions left by nonperiodic ergodic optimization. The result identifies explicit optimizers and reveals a rigorous arithmetic mechanism for unique periodic approximants, rather than computing arbitrary small cases or merely recomputing the global maximizing measure.
